title: Partisan Polarization Is the Primary Psychological Motivation behind Political Fake News Sharing on Twitter
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter-panel study (N=2,337 US Twitter users linked to scraped tweets) reporting quantitative shares with denominators: the share of tweeted news links coming from fake-news domains (3,269 of the tweeted news links, ~4%), the share of panelists who shared any fake-news link (11%), and a concentration statistic (top 1% of panelists = ~75% of all fake-news links). Aim is psychological motivation, but descriptive prevalence and concentration shares are reported in the Results.

estimates.date: Survey fielded mid-December 2018 to mid-January 2019; Twitter accounts scraped by early March 2019, tweets posted up to mid-January 2019 (~70% after the November 2016 election)
estimates.measure_type: % of news links tweeted/retweeted by panelists that came from domains with a history of publishing fake news
estimates.denominator: 85,344 tweeted news links (links to national news websites, fake or real) out of 2,709,052 tweets/retweets by 2,337 US Twitter panelists
estimates.definition: The tweeted URL's external web domain appears on a list of 608 fake news sources compiled by journalists and scholars (Guess et al. 2019; Allcott, Gentzkow and Yu 2019), i.e. domains known to publish factually incorrect news
estimates.misinfo_def: “fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent” (Lazer et al. 2018)
estimates.source_quote: Of the 2.7 million tweets in our data, only 85,344 (≈ 3%) contain links to national news websites, fake or real. Of the tweeted news links, 3,269 (≈ 4%) come from websites with a history of publishing fake news (see Grinberg et al. 2019, for slightly larger estimates during the 2016 US presidential election).
estimates.page_loc: Results, “Do people share news from fake news sources?” (p. 15 of the accepted manuscript)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: List of 608 fake news source domains constructed by journalists and scholars (Guess et al. 2019; Allcott, Gentzkow and Yu 2019), updated since 2016; real news comparison list of 260 publishers from AllSides. Automated URL-to-domain matching, no human coding and no inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: we follow best practices (Guess, Nyhan and Reifler 2020, Grinberg et al. 2019, Lazer et al. 2018) and operationalize “sharing of fake news sources” as when panel members tweet or retweet URLs to external web domains known to publish factually incorrect news. To this end, we cross-referenced all tweeted URLs against a list of 608 fake news sources, constructed by journalists and scholars
estimates.notes: Denominator is shared news links (national news websites, fake or real), hence news_diet rather than political_news: the fake-news list is political but the denominator is not restricted to political stories. Slight internal inconsistency in the paper: the news-link total is given as 85,344 here and as 85,084 in the headline-scraping section; the 4% is the paper's own verbatim figure (3,269/85,344 = 3.8%). Publisher-level, not story-level: the authors state “we cannot tell if the specific stories people share are true or false: Our fake news measure is at the publisher level, not the story level.”

estimates.date: Survey fielded mid-December 2018 to mid-January 2019; tweets scraped by early March 2019 covering tweets posted up to mid-January 2019
estimates.measure_type: % of Twitter panelists who shared at least one story from a fake news source during the study period
estimates.value_raw: only 11% of our participants shared stories from fake news sources
estimates.denominator: 2,337 US Twitter users recruited from the YouGov standing web panel whose public Twitter data could be linked
estimates.definition: Panelist tweeted or retweeted at least one URL to a domain on the 608-domain fake news source list during the observed period
estimates.misinfo_def: “fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent” (Lazer et al. 2018)
estimates.source_quote: Like others, and in contrast to what some commentators have feared, we find that only 11% of our participants shared stories from fake news sources during our period of study while half of the participants shared stories from real news web domains.
estimates.page_loc: Discussion (p. 31 of the accepted manuscript); also stated in Results as “11% of them are responsible for sharing all fake news sources” (p. 15)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: List of 608 fake news source domains constructed by journalists and scholars (Guess et al. 2019; Allcott, Gentzkow and Yu 2019); automated URL-to-domain matching, no inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: YouGov invited over 27,000 U.S. Twitter users from their standing web panel to participate in our study. 8,741 participants accepted the invitation and answered all questions before the final prompt to give consent to link their public Twitter data to the survey. ... Consequently, our final sample size is N = 2,337.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR NOTE: this is a behavioural share of PEOPLE who shared misinformation at least once, so it could equally be coded REACH with reach_subtype=sharing. I coded SHARING/actor_share because the instructions define actor_share explicitly as “% of users who shared any” and the paper frames it as sharing behaviour. Sample is a self-selected subset of a web panel with high, non-random attrition (2,337 of 8,741 who started), so not population-representative.

estimates.date: Tweets posted up to mid-January 2019 (majority after the November 2016 election), scraped by early March 2019
estimates.measure_type: share of all shared fake-news links accounted for by the top 1% of panelists
estimates.value_raw: 1% of the panelists are responsible for sharing about 75% of all links to fake news publishers
estimates.denominator: 3,269 links to fake news publishers shared by 2,337 US Twitter panelists
estimates.definition: Cumulative share of all shared fake-news-publisher links attributable to the most active 1% of the 2,337 panelists (empirical cumulative distribution function, Figure 1 left panel)
estimates.misinfo_def: “fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent” (Lazer et al. 2018)
estimates.source_quote: The left-hand panel in Figure 1 below makes clear that sharing content from fake news sources flourishes mostly among small segments of the population: 1% of the panelists are responsible for sharing about 75% of all links to fake news publishers and 11% of them are responsible for sharing all fake news sources.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 608-domain fake news source list (Guess et al. 2019; Allcott, Gentzkow and Yu 2019); automated matching of tweeted URLs.
estimates.moderator_quote: Note. The x-axes show percentage of participants responsible for sharing a given percentage of all news links (y-axes). ... (NFake News = 3,269; NReal News = 78,400)
estimates.notes: The paper also gives the parallel real-news concentration (top 1% = ~30% of real news shares), which is not a misinformation estimate, and a second misinformation concentration point (11% of panelists account for 100% of fake news shares) that is simply the complement of the actor-share row above; neither extracted.

estimates.date: Tweets posted up to mid-January 2019, scraped by early March 2019
estimates.measure_type: % of the shared fake-news links that came from “black” sources publishing almost exclusively fabricated stories
estimates.value_raw: about 30% of the fake news links come from sources “publishing almost exclusively fabricated stories”
estimates.denominator: 3,269 shared links to fake news publishers (a misinformation-only sample)
estimates.definition: Shared fake-news link whose domain is classified “black” in Grinberg et al. (2019), i.e. a source publishing almost exclusively fabricated stories
estimates.misinfo_def: “fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent” (Lazer et al. 2018)
estimates.source_quote: SM Section 8 uses Grinberg and colleagues’ (2019) fine-grained categorization of fake news sources and find that about 30% of the fake news links come from sources “publishing almost exclusively fabricated stories” (i.e. “black” sites).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) three-tier (black/red/orange) classification of fake news domains applied to the shared links.
estimates.moderator_quote: Importantly, not all fake news is equally troublesome. SM Section 8 uses Grinberg and colleagues’ (2019) fine-grained categorization of fake news sources
estimates.notes: R3 row: falsity tier computed INSIDE the misinformation-only sample of shared fake-news links, so within_misinfo_content=true (appendix only). The paper also states 5% come from “red” sites and two-thirds from “orange” sites; only the strictest (fabricated/black) tier is extracted to avoid redundant within-misinfo rows. NOT combinable with the 4% row into a stricter overall prevalence without computing a product, which R8 forbids.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) “only 85,344 (≈ 3%) contain links to national news websites, fake or real” — a share of news links among all tweets, not a misinformation share; (b) “half of the participants shared stories from real news web domains” and the real-news concentration (top 1% = ~30% of real-news shares) — real news, not misinformation; (c) “almost 86% of all shared fake news sources originated from one of these 42 domains” — a within-misinfo composition statistic about which domains have partisan ratings, not a falsity share; (d) “Another 5% come from sites that spread falsehoods that clearly reflected a flawed editorial process” and “two-thirds of the links referred to fake news sources where annotators were less certain” — further within-misinfo tiers, redundant with the extracted black-site row; (e) the 60% pro-Democratic / 23% pro-Republican split of REAL news shares; (f) the second concentration statement “11% of them are responsible for sharing all fake news sources” — identical information to the 11% actor-share row; (g) the sub-counts 2,563 pro-Republican and 263 pro-Democratic fake-news links, which the paper never expresses as a share of the news-link denominator (computing 2,563/85,344 would be an uncomputed part/whole the paper does not state as such — defensible under R8 but the partisan split is a moderator of the same estimate, not a distinct platform/country/measure cell, so no sub-rows were invented). Supplementary materials (SM Sections 5-12) were not available in this text file, so figures reported only there could not be checked.

rob.design: US Twitter users recruited from YouGov's standing web panel: over 27,000 invited, 8,741 completed the survey, 5,725 declined to give a Twitter ID, 639 IDs were inaccessible, final N = 2,337 (high, acknowledged non-random attrition; no response rate reported for the panel itself). Survey fielded mid-Dec 2018 to mid-Jan 2019, accounts scraped by early March 2019; 2,709,052 tweets/retweets. Misinformation coding is automated domain matching against a 608-domain fake-news list (journalist/scholar-compiled) plus a 260-publisher AllSides real-news list; no human coding, no inter-coder reliability statistics; robustness checks with the Grinberg et al. (2019) tier list, an alternative overlapping fake-news list, and Pennycook & Rand (2019a) trust ratings of 60 sources.
